text: Jacek Karpiński was a Polish computer scientist and engineer born in 1927 in Turin, Italy, into a family of intellectuals and alpinists. After losing his father in a Himalayan expedition and surviving a severe injury during World War II, he joined the Home Army and participated in resistance activities, including the Warsaw Uprising, for which he was awarded the Cross of Valour three times. Post-war, he studied engineering at Łódź and Warsaw University of Technology, graduating in 1951. He began his career at the Polish Academy of Sciences' Institute of Automatics, where he developed the AKAT-1, the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer, and later the AAH, a device for Fourier integral calculations. His success led to a UNESCO scholarship in the United States, where he met leading computer scientists like Claude Shannon. Inspired by his American experience, he designed a perceptron in 1964, one of the first in the world and the first in the Communist bloc. Despite moderate support and political opposition, Karpiński pursued his vision for a minicomputer, K-202, which was innovative and faster than competitors like the PDP-11. However, the project failed due to administrative issues, lack of political backing, and sabotage, with only 30 units produced. He later moved to Switzerland to work on Nagra tape recorders and returned to Poland, advising on computer science. Karpiński also worked as a secret informant for the Służba Bezpieczeństwa, collecting technological data. He died in 2010. His work is credited with significant technological achievements, though its full impact remains debated due to political and historical factors.
